newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week-Gilts to stay under U.S. thumb.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week-Gilts to stay under U.S. thumb.

text.p: UK gilts have some domestic excitement to capture their attention this week, with a monetary meeting on Wednesday, but events in the U.S. may still manage to eclipse the home news and exert a stronger influence.
Analysts said the combination of a two-day Federal Open Market Committee starting on Tuesday and crucial non-farm payroll data on Friday could steal the show.
"We have our own monetary meeting here for gilts to focus on, but international events will still dominate," said Huw Roberts, bond strategist at NatWest Markets.

International bond markets are most fearful that a decision to keep U.S. rates on hold will be swiftly followed by strong payroll and earnings numbers, making the authorities appear to be behind the curve.
A Reuter poll found 25 out of 26 economists expect U.S. rates to stay on hold, despite the recent spurt in growth.
GDP data out last Friday showed growth shot up by 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter, but the agony for U.S. Treasuries was offset by a small 1.8 percent rise in the GDP price index.
"There is some risk the Fed will go ahead and raise rates after the GDP data, but our central view is they will leave them on hold this time," said James McKay, UK economist at PaineWebber.

If rates are left unchanged, bond markets could get very jumpy in the run up to the January non-farm payroll data release at 1230 GMT on Friday. The consensus forecast suggests a rise of 237,000 compared with 262,000 in December.
But it will not be a wholly U.S. story this week and gilts will be able to claim some independence.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George meet to discuss monetary policy on Wednesday morning.

George has made clear he wants rates to rise by half a point from 6.0 percent to keep future inflation in check. But a Reuters poll found only one out of 24 economists polled expect Clarke to give in and sanction a rise.

This could be good news for gilts. "If we don't get a rise, there is a good chance gilts will rally, led by the short end. It will look like Clarke has won the day and there will be no rate rises before the election," said Roberts.
He believes there is scope for the yield curve to flatten, although that may have to wait until after the election.
"There is probably a flattening bias looking ahead, given the high chance that whoever wins the election they will raise rates aggressively, but that may be on hold for a while."

Most economists now forecast Clarke will not give in to George's requests for a rate rise until the election, which must be held by May. The opposition Labour party leads the ruling Conservatives by around 20 points in the opinion polls.
McKay said that in the meantime, the yield curve could actually steepen a bit further.

"There is a weakening trend across bond markets in Europe that gilts will fall prey to. And given that the pressure appears to be off interest rates short term, the curve could now steepen a bit," said McKay. However, he said the chances are slim that gilts will outperform major markets this week.
The spread narrowed to 179 basis points on Monday from 182 on Friday, but this could soon be reversed, traders said.
"I don't think there is any chance at all gilts will outperform this week. The only consolation is once the spread nears 200 it pulls in the buyers," said a gilts trader at a GEMM.

He added that the market may get a modest boost from December manufacturing data due on Thursday. The consensus forecast suggests output grew by 0.3 percent in December, leaving the year-on-year growth rate at a soft 1.2 percent.
"The manufacturing data has recently tended to show the recovery is still patchy and the pound's strength is keeping a check on things -- all good stuff for gilts."
